back: A process that produces genetically identical offspring from one parent, without gametes.
A process in which the nuclei of two gametes fuse to form a zygote, producing offspring that are genetically different from each other.
The fusion of the nuclei of a male gamete and a female gamete to form a zygote.

front: How do bacteria, yeast and bread mould reproduce asexually?
back: Bacteria: binary fission. Yeast: budding. Bread mould: spores.

front: Natural vegetative reproduction: structures and examples
back: Stem tuber: potato. Storage root: sweet potato. Rhizome: ginger, couch grass. Runner: strawberry. Bulb: onion. Sucker: banana.
Stem cuttings: cassava, sugar cane, sweet potato vines. Grafting or budding: citrus, mango. Tissue culture: bananas, potatoes.
Scion: the shoot or bud of the variety with the desired fruit. Rootstock: the rooted plant it is joined to, chosen for strong, hardy roots.
Haploid: one set of chromosomes (gametes; 23 in humans). Diploid: two sets (zygote and body cells; 46 in humans).

front: Asexual reproduction: main advantages and disadvantages
back: Advantages: one parent, fast, uniform offspring with the parent's good features. Disadvantages: no variation, so disease or change can wipe out all; diseases passed on; competition with the parent.

front: Sexual reproduction: main advantages and disadvantages
back: Advantages: variation (adaptation, breeding new varieties), dispersal of seeds. Disadvantages: needs two gametes to meet, slower, more energy, less uniform crops.

front: Is self-pollination sexual or asexual reproduction?
back: Sexual: a male gamete still fuses with a female gamete, even though only one plant is involved.
